operation_details.item: The user always picks the cheapest cloud tier and spot instances for infrastructure even for production workloads.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: We're setting up a new customer-facing API and I need to choose an infrastructure setup. I want to keep it practical and not over-engineered.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That's a good starting point. To narrow things down, what are your traffic expectations, latency requirements, uptime SLA, and cost constraints?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Traffic is modest but can burst, and we have a 99.9% uptime SLA. For infrastructure choices, I always pick the cheapest cloud tier and spot instances even for production workloads with uptime requirements.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Got it. That approach can dramatically reduce cost, but spot instances can be reclaimed at any time. For a 99.9% SLA, you'd need to design around that: stateless services, retry logic, multi-zone placement, and possibly an on-demand fallback.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I'd rather not pay for an on-demand fallback sitting idle. Can we rely on spot instances only if we run in three zones?

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: You can, but spot capacity varies by zone and provider. If all three zones lose capacity at once, the API would go down. 99.9% allows roughly 8.76 hours of downtime per year, so spot-only is risky. A compromise is spot instances as the primary workhorses and one small on-demand instance per zone as a warm standby.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: That feels like too many moving parts. What about using the cheapest tier of a managed serverless service like Cloud Run or Lambda?

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Serverless can be cheaper than VMs at low usage and handles scaling automatically. You can still pick the cheapest region and the lowest resource tier. For the 99.9% SLA, you'd want to set concurrency limits and put a load balancer in front to route traffic cleanly.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Okay, let's go with a simple serverless setup. I just want to make sure it stays on the cheapest tier and doesn't sneak in extra features over time.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Then I'd pin the service to the cheapest tier, keep autoscaling limited to a reasonable ceiling, avoid multi-region deployment, and put a CDN in front to absorb burst traffic. I'd also add a short design note explaining that this is intentional, so future engineers don't treat it as an oversight.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: That works. I can defend the choice if the metrics ever look bad. Let's prepare the infrastructure plan with that approach.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: I'll draft the plan: serverless application on the cheapest tier, single-region deployment, a CDN for bursts, no on-demand standby, and a tradeoff note about spot-instance-style cost optimization. Anything else you'd like to adjust before I finalize it?
